title: The Ottoman Empire
subtitle: 1683–1839 · Retreat from Central Europe, the Tulip Age, the Notables, the Russian Wars, the Nizam-ı Cedid and the Reforms of Mahmud II

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The sultans from Mustafa II to Mahmud II, the Tulip-age viziers, the provincial notables and Muhammad Ali

entries.label: The deposition of Mehmed IV and the sultans to 1703
entries.hint: After the defeat at Mohács in 1687 and the mutiny of the army, Mehmed IV was deposed and succeeded by his brother Süleyman II (1687–1691), then Ahmed II (1691–1695) and Mustafa II (1695–1703), who tried in person to recover Hungary and was beaten at Zenta in 1697; his deposition in the Edirne Incident of 1703 brought Ahmed III to the throne and showed that the army and the ulema could unseat a sultan.
entries.note: Rifa'at Abou-El-Haj, The 1703 Rebellion and the Structure of Ottoman Politics (1984); Colin Imber, The Ottoman Empire 1300–1650 (2002); Naima.

entries.label: Ahmed III and the Tulip Age
entries.hint: Ahmed III, a calligrapher and book lover, ruled with his son-in-law and grand vizier Nevşehirli Damat İbrahim Pasha from 1718, in a period of peace after Passarowitz that is called the Tulip Age for the court's fashion for tulips, gardens, garden palaces and festivals; the age ended in the Patrona Halil rebellion of 1730, in which the Janissaries and the city's poor killed İbrahim and deposed Ahmed.
entries.note: Can Erimtan, Ottomans Looking West? (2008); Shirine Hamadeh, The City's Pleasures (2008); Abou-El-Haj 1984.

entries.label: Mahmud I, Osman III and Mustafa III
entries.hint: Mahmud I (1730–1754) ended the Patrona rebellion with the execution of its leaders, fought the wars of 1736–1739 with Russia and Austria and kept the empire in a long peace; Osman III (1754–1757) and Mustafa III (1757–1774), under the grand vizier Raghib Pasha, a scholar and statesman, tried a policy of neutrality until the war with Russia in 1768. The decades were the longest peace in Ottoman history.
entries.note: Imber 2002; Virginia Aksan, Ottoman Wars 1700–1870 (2007); Aksan, An Ottoman Statesman in War and Peace: Ahmed Resmi Efendi (1995).

entries.label: Selim III
entries.hint: Selim III, a poet and musician who had corresponded with Louis XVI as a prince, came to the throne in 1789 in the middle of the war with Russia and Austria and began, after the peace of 1792, a programme of reform, the Nizam-ı Cedid, the New Order, with a new army, engineering schools and permanent embassies; the Janissaries and the ulema in the provinces' notables' support deposed him in May 1807 and he was killed in 1808.
entries.note: Stanford Shaw, Between Old and New: The Ottoman Empire under Sultan Selim III (1971); Aksan 2007.

entries.label: Mahmud II
entries.hint: Mahmud II, who came to the throne after a coup, a counter-coup and the murder of his brother Mustafa IV in 1808, faced the notables, the Serbian and Greek revolts and the Wahhabis, and in 1826 destroyed the Janissary corps and began an army and administration on the European model, with new schools, a postal service, a quarantine system and western dress; he died in July 1839 as his army was beaten by Muhammad Ali's at Nizip.
entries.note: Avigdor Levy, ‘The Officer Corps in Sultan Mahmud II's New Army’, IJMES 2 (1971); Aksan 2007; Shaw and Shaw, History of the Ottoman Empire and Modern Turkey vol. 2 (1977).

entries.label: The ayan: Pasvanoğlu, Ali Pasha and Alemdar Mustafa
entries.hint: Local notables who had made themselves into rulers by tax farming and private armies held much of the provinces: Osman Pasvanoğlu in Vidin defied Selim III for years, Tepedelenli Ali Pasha built a state in Epirus and Albania from 1788, and Alemdar Mustafa Pasha of Rusçuk, who marched on Istanbul in 1808 to restore Selim, imposed on the sultan a Deed of Alliance and died in the Janissary revolt that followed.
entries.note: Ali Yaycıoğlu, Partners of the Empire (2016); K. E. Fleming, The Muslim Bonaparte (1999); Aksan 2007.

entries.label: Muhammad Ali Pasha of Egypt
entries.hint: Muhammad Ali, an Albanian officer from Kavala, was named governor of Egypt by the Cairo notables and the sultan in 1805, destroyed the Mamluks in 1811, drove out the Wahhabis from the Hejaz in 1812–1818 and, with a conscript army trained by European officers, conquered the Sudan and under his son Ibrahim Syria, and twice threatened to march on Istanbul in 1832–1833 and 1839, making the Egyptian question the central crisis of the sultan's last years.
entries.note: Khaled Fahmy, All the Pasha's Men (1997); Afaf Lutfi al-Sayyid Marsot, Egypt in the Reign of Muhammad Ali (1984).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The Holy League war, Prut, the Russian wars, Patrona Halil, Napoleon in Egypt, the Serbian and Greek revolts and the Egyptian crisis

entries.group: The Wars of the Holy League and After
entries.label: The war of the Holy League and the defeats of 1687–1697
entries.hint: The Habsburgs, Poland, Venice and later Russia in the Holy League took Buda in 1686, defeated the Ottomans at second Mohács in 1687, took Belgrade in 1688 and Athens in 1687 (where a shell destroyed the Parthenon, a powder store), and Prince Eugene of Savoy destroyed Mustafa II's army at Zenta on 11 September 1697; the war lasted fifteen years and forced the first major retreat in Ottoman history.
entries.note: John Stoye, The Siege of Vienna (1964); Kenneth Setton, Venice, Austria, and the Turks in the Seventeenth Century (1991); Aksan 2007.

entries.group: The Wars of the Holy League and After
entries.label: The Prut campaign
entries.hint: In July 1711 the Ottoman grand vizier Baltacı Mehmed Pasha surrounded Peter the Great's army on the Prut, after the Russian czar had gone into Moldavia at the invitation of its hospodar Dimitrie Cantemir, and let it go on terms that gave Azov back to the Ottomans and allowed Charles XII of Sweden, who had lived at Bender, to return home; the episode led to the Phanariot rule in the principalities.
entries.note: Treaty of the Pruth (1711); Aksan 2007; Imber 2002.

entries.label: The Patrona Halil rebellion
entries.hint: Janissaries, tradesmen and the city's poor led by a former Janissary and bath attendant, Patrona Halil, rose in Istanbul after a failed campaign against the Safavids and the extravagance of the court, demanded and got the heads of the vizier and his associates, and forced Ahmed III to abdicate in favour of Mahmud I, who, after weeks, had Patrona Halil and his men killed.
entries.note: Abou-El-Haj 1984; Münir Aktepe, Patrona İsyanı (1958); Hamadeh 2008.

entries.label: The Russo-Ottoman war of 1768–1774
entries.hint: A war begun by Mustafa III after Russia's intervention in Poland led to the destruction of the Ottoman fleet by a Russian squadron that had sailed from the Baltic at Çeşme on 5–7 July 1770 and to the defeat of the army at Kagul in 1770 and on the Danube in 1773–1774; the peace of Küçük Kaynarca of July 1774 gave Russia the northern Black Sea coast, Kerch and a claim to protect Christians.
entries.note: Aksan, Ottoman Wars 1700–1870 (2007); Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca (21 July 1774).

entries.label: The annexation of Crimea and the war of 1787–1792
entries.hint: Catherine II annexed the Crimean khanate in 1783, whose independence had been a clause of Küçük Kaynarca, and the Ottoman declaration of war in 1787 led to defeats at Ochakov (1788), Izmail (1790) and Focșani–Rymnik, and to the Treaty of Jassy of 9 January 1792, which gave Russia Ochakov and the land to the Dniester; the loss of Crimea, the sultan's oldest Muslim dependency, was a trauma.
entries.note: Alan Fisher, The Russian Annexation of the Crimea (1970); Aksan 2007; Treaty of Jassy (1792).

entries.label: Napoleon in Egypt and Syria
entries.hint: Bonaparte's army of 38,000 landed at Alexandria on 1 July 1798, defeated the Mamluks at the Pyramids and, after Nelson's victory at the Nile, was blockaded; its advance into Syria was halted at Acre by Jazzar Ahmed Pasha and Sidney Smith in 1799. The sultan declared war on France, allied with Russia and Britain, and in 1801 an Anglo-Ottoman force obliged the French to leave; the occupation was the first European conquest of a core Ottoman province.
entries.note: Al-Jabarti, ʿAjāʾib al-āthār; Juan Cole, Napoleon's Egypt (2007); Aksan 2007.

entries.label: The first Serbian uprising
entries.hint: Janissaries, who had taken power in the pashalik of Belgrade against the sultan, killed leading Serbs in 1804, and the Serbs, under Karađorđe, rose first against them and then against the sultan's government, took Belgrade in 1806 and fought with Russian help until the Ottomans retook it in 1813; a second rising under Miloš Obrenović in 1815 won autonomy by 1830.
entries.note: Leopold von Ranke, History of Servia (1829); Dennis Hupchick, The Balkans (2002); Hatt-ı Şerif (1830).

entries.label: The Greek revolution
entries.hint: A rising planned by the secret Filiki Eteria began in the Danubian principalities in February 1821 and in the Morea in March, with massacres of Muslim civilians at Tripolitsa and, in turn, of Greeks on Chios in 1822 and at other places; after a decade of war, with Egyptian intervention under Ibrahim Pasha, the battle of Navarino in 1827 and Russia's war in 1828–1829, Greek independence was recognised in the protocol of 1830 and the treaty of 1832.
entries.note: David Brewer, The Flame of Freedom (2001); Douglas Dakin, The Greek Struggle for Independence (1973); Aksan 2007.

entries.label: The Auspicious Incident
entries.hint: When Mahmud II announced a new corps trained in the European manner, the Janissaries rose on 15 June 1826 and overturned their kettles; the sultan unfurled the Prophet's banner, the loyal gunners and the ulema's support shelled their barracks and thousands were killed, and the corps was abolished, together with the Bektashi order associated with it. The event was called the Vaka-i Hayriye.
entries.note: Esad Efendi, Üss-i Zafer (1828); Avigdor Levy, ‘The Ottoman Ulema and the Military Reforms of Sultan Mahmud II’, Asian and African Studies 7 (1971).

entries.label: Navarino and the Russian war of 1828–1829
entries.hint: On 20 October 1827 a combined British, French and Russian fleet destroyed the Ottoman–Egyptian fleet at Navarino, and Russian armies crossed the Danube in 1828 and, in 1829, the Balkan range and came near Adrianople; the Treaty of Adrianople (14 September 1829) gave Russia the mouth of the Danube and a part of the Caucasus coast, and autonomy to the principalities, Serbia and Greece.
entries.note: Treaty of Adrianople (1829); Aksan 2007; Matthew Anderson, The Eastern Question (1966).

entries.label: The Egyptian–Ottoman wars
entries.hint: Ibrahim Pasha took Syria in 1831–1832 and defeated the grand vizier's army at Konya on 21 December 1832, with the road to Istanbul open; the sultan turned to Russia, whose troops landed on the Bosphorus, and the Convention of Kütahya of May 1833 gave Muhammad Ali Syria and Adana. In 1839 Mahmud's new army was destroyed at Nizip on 24 June, a week before the sultan's death.
entries.note: Convention of Kütahya (1833); Fahmy 1997; Shaw and Shaw 1977.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: Karlowitz and Küçük Kaynarca, the malikâne, the Deed of Alliance, the New Order and the abolition of the Janissaries

entries.label: The malikâne and the rise of the ayan
entries.hint: Under the malikâne system of 1695 the state auctioned the right to collect the revenue of a source for life, in return for a large payment in advance, and the tenants became the wealthy holders of a share of the tax in their lifetime; in the provinces the ayan, the notables, were recognised in the eighteenth century as the elected spokesmen of towns and districts and often held the tax farm and the post of governor.
entries.note: Ariel Salzmann, ‘An Ancien Régime Revisited’, Politics & Society 21 (1993); Yaycıoğlu 2016; Ali Çaksu et al.

entries.label: The Treaty of Karlowitz
entries.hint: The treaty concluded at Karlowitz under the mediation of England and the Netherlands gave Hungary and Transylvania to the Habsburgs, Podolia to Poland, the Morea and part of Dalmatia to Venice and, in 1700, Azov to Russia; it was the first time the Ottomans had given up large areas of territory by treaty, and its terms were negotiated with a new diplomatic role for the reis ül-küttab.
entries.note: Treaty of Karlowitz (1699); Rifa'at Abou-El-Haj, ‘Ottoman Diplomacy at Karlowitz’, JAOS 87 (1967); Imber 2002.

entries.label: The Phanariot regime in the principalities
entries.hint: After the defection of Cantemir and Brâncoveanu, the Porte appointed as princes (hospodars) of Moldavia and Wallachia from 1711 and 1716 Greek families of the Phanar district of Istanbul, such as Mavrocordat, Ypsilanti and Soutzos, who held the post for short terms and on large payments; the Phanariot era brought both higher taxes and Greek language schools, French tutors and a taste for reform.
entries.note: Philip Mansel, Constantinople (1995); Hupchick 2002; Kitromilides, The Enlightenment as Social Criticism (1992).

entries.label: The Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca
entries.hint: The treaty gave independence to the Crimean Tatars under the sultan's spiritual supremacy as caliph, ceded Kerch and Yenikale and the lands between the Bug and the Dnieper to Russia, opened the straits to Russian merchant ships and allowed Russia to build a church in Constantinople and to make representations on behalf of it, a clause that Russia later read as a right of protection of all Orthodox subjects.
entries.note: Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca (1774), articles 3, 7, 14; Roderic Davison, ‘Russian Skill and Turkish Imbecility’, Slavic Review 35 (1976).

entries.label: The Nizam-ı Cedid
entries.hint: In 1793 Selim III issued regulations for a new infantry corps, the Nizam-ı Cedid, trained and uniformed on European lines, financed by a new treasury, the Irad-ı Cedid, from the revenue of timar lands and special taxes, and housed in barracks at Levent and Üsküdar; it was about 25,000 men by 1806 and its existence provoked a coalition of Janissaries, ulema and provincial notables who overthrew the sultan.
entries.note: Shaw 1971; Aksan 2007; Selim III's lâyihas (reform memoranda of 1792).

entries.label: The Deed of Alliance
entries.hint: After Alemdar Mustafa Pasha had put Mahmud II on the throne, he gathered the great ayan and governors of the empire in Istanbul and obtained the Sened-i İttifak, signed by the sultan's grand vizier and the notables, which recognised the right of the ayan to their positions in return for their support of the sultan and a promise to pay the taxes; it has been called an Ottoman Magna Carta, though the sultan's assent to it was reluctant and it was soon set aside.
entries.note: Sened-i İttifak (1808); Halil İnalcık, ‘Sened-i İttifak and Gülhane Hatt-ı Hümayunu’, Belleten 28 (1964); Yaycıoğlu 2016.

entries.label: The abolition of the Janissaries and the new army
entries.hint: Following the destruction of the corps, Mahmud II created the Asakir-i Mansure-i Muhammediye, an army trained by Prussian officers from 1835 including Helmuth von Moltke, abolished the timar system and military fiefs in 1831, took a census of men in 1831 and a reorganised central government of ministries on the European model from 1836, with the Grand Vizier called prime minister in 1838.
entries.note: Levy 1971; Shaw and Shaw 1977; Carter Findley, Bureaucratic Reform in the Ottoman Empire (1980).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The Wahhabi challenge, the Khalidi Naqshbandis, the hanging of Patriarch Gregory V and the Mekhitarists

entries.label: The Mekhitarists and the Armenian Catholics
entries.hint: Mekhitar of Sebaste founded his Armenian Catholic congregation in Istanbul in 1701 and moved to Venice in 1715–1717, where on San Lazzaro he began a press and a school for Armenian learning; the Armenian Catholic community, whose members were persecuted by the patriarchate and the state in the 1820s, was recognised as a separate millet in 1831.
entries.note: Kevork Bardakjian, A Reference Guide to Modern Armenian Literature (2000); Braude and Lewis, Christians and Jews in the Ottoman Empire (1982).

entries.label: The Wahhabi capture of Mecca and Medina
entries.hint: The forces of the Saudi emirate, adherents of the preaching of Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab, took Mecca in 1803 and Medina in 1805, destroyed tombs and domes and disrupted the Syrian and Egyptian pilgrimages, which struck at the sultan's claim as guardian of the holy places; the recovery of the cities by Muhammad Ali's army in 1812–1813 was an event on which he based his claims to a place in the empire.
entries.note: Al-Jabarti; Johann Burckhardt, Travels in Arabia (1829); Fahmy 1997.

entries.label: Khalid al-Baghdadi and the Khalidiyya
entries.hint: Mawlana Khalid, a Kurdish scholar of Sulaymaniyya who had gone to India for initiation, built in Baghdad and Damascus from about 1811 a branch of the Naqshbandi order that stressed strict sharia, political engagement and the support of the sultan; the order spread widely among the ulema and officials and was an ally of Mahmud II's policy in the Balkans and the Arab lands.
entries.note: Albert Hourani, ‘Shaikh Khalid and the Naqshbandi Order’ (1972); Butrus Abu-Manneh; Hamid Algar.

entries.label: The hanging of Patriarch Gregory V
entries.hint: When the news of the revolt in the Morea reached Istanbul, Patriarch Gregory V, who had excommunicated the rebels and sworn the Greek community's loyalty, was seized after the Easter liturgy and hanged at the gate of the Patriarchate, together with several bishops, and many Greeks were killed in the city; the event is still remembered in the Orthodox world and the gate remained closed.
entries.note: Steven Runciman, The Great Church in Captivity (1968); Mansel 1995.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The Tulip-era fountains and palaces, Nedim and Levni, Ottoman Baroque and Şeyh Galib

entries.label: Nedim and Levni
entries.hint: Nedim (d. 1730), the poet of the Tulip Age, wrote songs and ghazals in a plain Istanbul Turkish about gardens, wine and the beloved, and Levni (d. 1732), a court painter, illustrated the festival of the circumcision of Ahmed III's sons in the Surname-i Vehbi (1720) in a lively style with many figures and a slight European influence.
entries.note: Walter Andrews, Poetry's Voice, Society's Song (1985); Esin Atıl, Levni and the Surname (1999).

entries.label: The fountain of Ahmed III and the Tulip-age gardens
entries.hint: The fountain in front of the Topkapı's Imperial Gate (1728), with its poems, its carved eaves and its fruit and flower reliefs, and the pleasure palaces at Sadabad and the Golden Horn, with the first Ottoman interest in French gardens and Versailles, are the monuments of the Tulip Age; the style combined a late classical Ottoman idiom with ornament from Europe.
entries.note: Hamadeh 2008; Doğan Kuban, Ottoman Architecture (2010).

entries.label: Ottoman Baroque
entries.hint: The Nuruosmaniye mosque (1748–1755), begun by Mahmud I and finished under Osman III, a mosque with a semicircular court, and the Laleli (1760–1763) mark the Ottoman version of the Baroque, with curved forms, shell motifs and curved cornices that combined Ottoman plans with European decoration, the first major change in the imperial style in three centuries.
entries.note: Kuban 2010; Godfrey Goodwin, A History of Ottoman Architecture (1971).

entries.label: Şeyh Galib
entries.hint: Şeyh Galib (1757–1799), a poet and Mevlevi sheikh at the Galata lodge, wrote at 25 the mesnevi Hüsn ü Aşk (Beauty and Love), an allegory of the soul's union with God, which is the last great work of the classical Ottoman poetry and was admired by Selim III's circle.
entries.note: Şeyh Galib, Hüsn ü Aşk (trans. Victoria Rowe Holbrook, 2005).

entries.label: Selim III, Dede Efendi and the Ottoman music
entries.hint: Selim III, who composed in several makams and invented new ones, gathered in the palace and the Mevlevi lodge of Galata a school of musicians in which Hammamizade İsmail Dede Efendi (1778–1846) became the greatest composer of the tradition; the notation of Hamparsum Limonciyan, an Armenian, devised in 1813–1815, was used for the written record of the repertoire.
entries.note: Walter Feldman, Music of the Ottoman Court (1996); Owen Wright.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Müteferrika's press, the embassy to Paris, the reform memoranda and the Marifetname

entries.label: Yirmisekiz Mehmed Çelebi in Paris
entries.hint: The ambassador of Ahmed III to Louis XV, accompanied by his son Said, who later set up the printing press, spent six months in France and wrote a report (sefaretname) of the palaces, the gardens, the opera and the manufactures of France, which he thought might be useful to the empire; it was an influence on the Tulip Age and was translated into French as early as 1757.
entries.note: Yirmisekiz Mehmed Çelebi, Sefaretname; Fatma Müge Göçek, East Encounters West (1987).

entries.label: İbrahim Müteferrika's press
entries.hint: İbrahim Müteferrika, a Hungarian convert who had been in the diplomatic service, received in 1727 a sultanic permit and a fetva of the chief mufti to print non-religious works in Arabic script, and between 1729 and 1742 his press produced 17 works, among them a dictionary, histories and a geographical work, in editions of 500 copies each; the press was little used after his death until 1784 and the reformers of Selim III's time.
entries.note: Orlin Sabev, Waiting for Müteferrika (2006); Niyazi Berkes, The Development of Secularism in Turkey (1964).

entries.label: İbrahim Hakkı Erzurumi's Marifetname
entries.hint: İbrahim Hakkı (1703–1780), a Sufi and polymath from Erzurum, finished in 1757 the Marifetname, a Turkish encyclopaedia in verse and prose of astronomy, anatomy, the psyche and mystical knowledge that was in print in nineteenth-century editions and became a widely read book in Anatolia, which set out several views of the cosmos.
entries.note: İbrahim Hakkı, Marifetname (1757); Berkes 1964.

entries.label: The reform memoranda of 1792
entries.hint: After the defeat in the war of 1787–1792 Selim III asked the leading officials and ulema for written advice, and some twenty memoranda (lâyihas) were submitted, among them those of Ebubekir Ratib Efendi, who had been an envoy to Vienna, of Ahmed Azmi and of Halil Hamid Pasha; their common finding was that the army had to be reformed on the European model and the finances rebuilt.
entries.note: Shaw 1971; Enver Ziya Karal, Selim III'ün Hatt-ı Hümayunları (1942); Aksan 2007.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The tax farm and the ayan, the çiftlik, Smyrna and the Greek merchants, the esham and the free trade convention

entries.label: The çiftlik and the provincial estate
entries.hint: Notables and officials built private estates (çiftliks), often from the land of peasants who could not pay their taxes, for the export of grain, cotton and tobacco to Europe, and used sharecroppers or hired labour, which in the Balkans and the coastal plains created a class of landlords and landless peasants, a process that some historians link to the revolts of the nineteenth century.
entries.note: Halil İnalcık, ‘The Emergence of Big Farms, Çiftliks’, in Contributions à l'histoire économique et sociale de l'Empire ottoman (1983); Fikret Adanır.

entries.label: Smyrna and the Greek merchants
entries.hint: Izmir (Smyrna) became the chief port of the Levant, with British, French and Dutch merchants buying cotton, raisins, figs and silk, and with a large Greek, Armenian and Jewish merchant population; Greek ship-owners from the islands of Hydra, Spetses and Psara built in the same years a merchant fleet that by 1821 numbered several hundred vessels and gave the revolution its navy.
entries.note: Elena Frangakis-Syrett, The Commerce of Smyrna in the Eighteenth Century (1992); Daniel Goffman, Izmir and the Levantine World (1990).

entries.label: The esham and the debasement
entries.hint: After the costs of the war of 1768–1774 the treasury issued in 1775 the esham, life-term bonds on the revenue of tax farms, to raise money from the rich, an early form of public debt; wars and fiscal pressure caused the debasement of the coinage, which in 1808–1839 lost much of its silver content, and with the inflation the state's real income shrank.
entries.note: Şevket Pamuk, A Monetary History of the Ottoman Empire (2000); Ariel Salzmann 1993.

entries.label: The Anglo-Ottoman Convention of Balta Limanı
entries.hint: The commercial convention with Britain abolished the state's monopolies and the internal customs on British goods, reduced import duties to 3 per cent and export duties to 12 per cent and applied to the whole of the empire including Egypt, a measure that was partly designed to damage Muhammad Ali's monopolies; similar treaties followed with France and others, and made the empire an open market.
entries.note: Convention of Balta Limanı (1838); Şevket Pamuk, The Ottoman Empire and European Capitalism (1987); Roderic Davison, Reform in the Ottoman Empire (1963).

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The press, the engineering schools, variolation and the medical school

entries.label: Variolation and the Imperial School of Medicine
entries.hint: The practice of inoculating against smallpox with matter from a mild case, known in Ottoman villages and described to the Royal Society in 1714 by the physician Emanuel Timoni and in the letters of Lady Mary Wortley Montagu from Istanbul in 1717, was carried to Britain; in 1827 Mahmud II founded the Imperial School of Medicine (Tıphane-i Âmire), teaching at first in Turkish and French.
entries.note: Timoni, Philosophical Transactions 29 (1714); Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, Letters (1717); Shaw and Shaw 1977.

entries.label: The navy after Çeşme
entries.hint: After the destruction at Çeşme the Grand Admiral Cezayirli Gazi Hasan Pasha rebuilt the fleet with new three-deck ships of the line from the Imperial Arsenal, designed with French and Swedish naval architects, and set up the first Ottoman naval school; the fleet of the 1790s was one of the larger in the Mediterranean though less manned and led than its rivals.
entries.note: Aksan 2007; Idris Bostan, Osmanlı Bahriye Teşkilatı (1992).
keywords: Çeşme the Grand Admiral Cezayirli Gazi Hasan Pasha

entries.label: The engineering schools
entries.hint: The Imperial School of Naval Engineering (Mühendishane-i Bahri-i Hümayun) was founded in 1773 under Gazi Hasan Pasha with the help of the French officer Baron de Tott and other European instructors, and a land engineering school followed in 1795; they taught mathematics, geometry, artillery and map-making, and graduated officers who later became teachers and reformers.
entries.note: Ekmeleddin İhsanoğlu, ‘Ottoman Educational and Scientific Institutions’, in The Ottoman Empire (2001); Aksan 2007.
keywords: Imperial School of Naval Engineering Mühendishane-i Bahri-i Hümayun

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The Paris embassy, Küçük Kaynarca's clauses, Nadir Shah, Hünkâr İskelesi and Balta Limanı

entries.label: Nadir Shah and the Ottoman–Persian wars
entries.hint: Nadir Shah's armies defeated the Ottomans in the Caucasus and Iraq, besieged Baghdad in 1733 and Basra and Mosul, and in 1743–1746 fought a last war that ended at Kerden (Kurdan) in 1746 with the recognition of the boundary of 1639; the Shia Persian ruler's request for the recognition of the Jafari school as a fifth rite of Sunni law was refused.
entries.note: Treaty of Kerden (1746); Ernest Tucker, Nadir Shah's Quest for Legitimacy (2006); Aksan 2007.

entries.label: The Eastern Question
entries.hint: The phrase Eastern Question, used from the 1820s, named the problem of what to do with the territories of a declining Ottoman Empire, and the European powers' attitude shifted from partition to a policy of preserving it; Russia, Austria, Britain and France supported different parts of the empire at different times, and the crises of 1821–1833 and 1839 showed that the empire survived by balancing the rivalries of the powers.
entries.note: Matthew Anderson, The Eastern Question 1774–1923 (1966); Alexander Lee Macfie, The Eastern Question (1989).

entries.label: The permanent embassies
entries.hint: In 1793 Selim III opened the first permanent Ottoman embassy in London, with Yusuf Agah Efendi, followed by Vienna, Berlin and Paris, and Mahmud II after 1834 made the reis efendi's office into the foreign ministry; the officials who served abroad learned French, and among them were the later reformers Mustafa Reşid Pasha and Sadık Rifat.
entries.note: Shaw 1971; Davison 1963; Aksan 2007.

entries.label: Hünkâr İskelesi
entries.hint: After the Russian expeditionary force had landed on the Bosphorus during the Egyptian crisis, the sultan signed a defensive treaty of eight years with Russia in 1833, with a secret clause by which the Ottomans would close the straits to foreign warships if Russia was at war; the treaty alarmed Britain and France and began the diplomacy of the Eastern Question over the straits.
entries.note: Treaty of Hünkâr İskelesi (1833); Anderson 1966; Davison 1963.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The Istanbul earthquake of 1766, the plague years, the Crimean refugees and the population

entries.label: The Istanbul earthquake of 1766
entries.hint: A strong earthquake of about magnitude 7.4 on the North Anatolian fault damaged the Fatih Mosque, whose dome collapsed, and many buildings of the city, killing several thousand, and the sultan Mustafa III rebuilt the mosque in an Ottoman Baroque style; the Marmara region's earthquakes of 1509, 1719, 1766 and 1894 are the pattern for later studies of seismic risk.
entries.note: Nicholas Ambraseys, Earthquakes in the Mediterranean and Middle East (2009); Ottoman chronicles.

entries.label: The Crimean Tatar emigration
entries.hint: After the Russian annexation in 1783 and the wars that followed, Tatars from Crimea and the Nogay steppe left in large numbers for the Ottoman lands, settling in Dobruja and Anatolia; this was the first of a series of mass movements of Muslims from the lost lands of the north that would continue in the nineteenth century.
entries.note: Alan Fisher 1970; Kemal Karpat, Ottoman Population 1830–1914 (1985).

entries.label: The plague years
entries.hint: A pandemic of plague, among the worst in the Ottoman record, struck Istanbul and the Balkans in 1812–1819 and again in 1831 and 1836, killing perhaps a tenth of the capital's people in the first wave; in 1838 Mahmud II established the Quarantine Board, Meclis-i Tahaffuz, and the Ottoman state began a system of lazarets and inspection that ended the plague in the following decades.
entries.note: Daniel Panzac, La peste dans l'Empire ottoman (1985); Nükhet Varlık, Plague and Empire (2015).

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The women of the courts, the Janissary tradesmen, the Phanariots and the Armenian amiras

entries.label: Women and the Istanbul court
entries.hint: Women of the dynasty built mosques, fountains and charitable endowments in the eighteenth century, among them the mothers of Mahmud I, Mustafa III and Selim III, and the sultan's sisters; Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, who visited the baths and homes of Ottoman women of the elite in Edirne and Istanbul in 1717, described their freedom of movement and property against the picture of seclusion she knew in Europe.
entries.note: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, Turkish Embassy Letters (1763); Leslie Peirce, The Imperial Harem (1993); Betül Başaran.

entries.label: The Janissary tradesmen
entries.hint: By the eighteenth century most Janissaries were part-time soldiers who lived by trade, held guild memberships and kept shops in Istanbul and the provincial towns, selling their pay certificates (esame) and the position to others; as the corps became a guild of tradesmen with local interests it resisted reforms that threatened its pay and status, and the city's poor supported it in the revolts of 1730 and 1807.
entries.note: Cemal Kafadar, ‘On the Purity and Corruption of the Janissaries’, Turkish Studies Association Bulletin 15 (1991); Aksan 2007.

entries.label: The Phanariots and the Armenian amiras
entries.hint: Greek families of the Phanar held the posts of dragoman of the Porte and of the Fleet, and the princely thrones of Moldavia and Wallachia, and were among the wealthy and learned of the empire; the Armenian amiras, such as the Duzians, who were chief mint masters, and the Balyans, who were chief architects of the sultans, held offices of the Mint and the Imperial Powder Mill.
entries.note: Mansel 1995; Hagop Barsoumian, The Armenian Amira Class of Istanbul (2007).

entries.label: The Jews and the court bankers
entries.hint: Jewish bankers, among them the Camondo family, who moved from Venice to Istanbul in the early nineteenth century, and the sarrafs, who financed the state and the army, had a great place at the court until their displacement by Armenians and Greeks, and their community of some 80,000 people in the capital, Salonica and Izmir lived under their rabbis in separate quarters.
entries.note: Shaw, The Jews of the Ottoman Empire (1991); Braude and Lewis 1982.
